column4: The source section names root د ع ع for the harsh shove in 107:2; here the same root describes deniers shoved toward Hell, turning the bodily action back on the one who pushes.
This neighboring ayah identifies the fire of 52:13 as the one they denied; it completes the reversed shove with its judgment setting.
The section names root ح ض ض as urging toward good and mutual prompting; this verse says they do not urge one another to the miskin's food, making the omitted encouragement explicit.
The section pairs pushing an orphan with failing to honor him; this verse names honoring the orphan as the contrary duty.
The section's pushed-away vulnerable person meets a direct boundary here: do not overpower the orphan.
The supplicant whom the section says is left without aid is met here by a prohibition on rebuffing the one who asks.
The section's root م ن ع means interposing between a person and what they want; this verse bars the miskin from entering the garden, giving that barrier a concrete scene.
The source section's root م ن ع describes stopping good from reaching someone; this verse calls a person a persistent preventer of good, making the section's blocked aid a moral trait.
The source section develops failure to urge food for the poor; this verse repeats that omission with the same root ح ض ض in a judgment scene.
The section sets motionless prayer beside withheld aid; this verse joins prayer performed lazily with showing off to people, a close parallel to the surah's paired prayer and display.
The section places prayer and material assistance in one image; this verse pairs lazy prayer with spending only unwillingly.
The section's stillness in prayer meets its direct counterpart here: the condemned say they were not among those who prayed; 74:44 gives the linked failure to feed the miskin.
This verse says they did not feed the miskin, pairing material neglect with the prayerlessness in 74:43 and the section.
The section frames conduct as denial of the Day of Judgment; this verse names denial of that Day among the reasons for the condemned group's fate.
The section pictures a body turning away from an orphan; this passage opens with a frown and turning away from a vulnerable visitor, a direct reversal of attentive care.
The next ayah identifies the visitor as blind; that detail makes the turning away in this ayah a refusal of someone physically vulnerable.
This ayah asks whether the visitor might purify himself; 80:8-9 later says he came striving and fearing, showing why attention to him mattered.
The visitor may take a reminder; this supplies the useful outcome that the earlier frown and turn-away interrupts.
This verse introduces the self-sufficient person, setting the status contrast that explains why attention shifts away from the needy visitor.
The addressee attends to the self-sufficient person, exposing status-driven attention in the same scene of neglect.
This ayah says the addressee is not accountable if the self-sufficient person does not purify himself; 80:8-10 returns attention to the one who comes seeking.
The section's weak person is turned away; here the weak visitor comes running, and 80:9 adds that he fears God.
The visitor's fear is named here, completing the reason his approach merits attention after the prior ayat describe turning toward the rich.
This closing rebuke returns to turning away from the earnest seeker, directly reversing the section's shove and neglect.
The section shows the weak left exposed; this verse forbids driving away worshippers who call on God morning and evening, and names doing so as wrongdoing.
The next ayah says people are tested by one another's relative standing; it adds the status question behind the command not to dismiss low-status worshippers in 6:52.

This verse says to remain with those who call on God and not turn one's eyes away from them, while warning against following a heedless heart; it meets the section's still prayer-heart and rejected needy person in one scene.
The section's root gloss pictures need as arresting motion; here the poor are explicitly described as constrained and unable to travel the land, giving that image a concrete Quranic counterpart.

The section invokes س ك ن's stillness branch for the miskin; this ayah calls the poor people working at sea and shows their livelihood being protected, a limit on treating the image as a definition of all poor people.
The section says orphanhood removes a protective ring; here a wall preserves two orphans' property until they mature, a direct counter-scene of protection.
This ayah directs giving to the miskin; it reverses the section's blocked small aid by assigning the needy a share from one's resources.
This inheritance scene directs that poor people and orphans present receive a provision and kind words; it joins aid with speech toward the vulnerable.
The section says the person does not even urge others to feed the poor; this verse directs a gentle word when help cannot be given, preserving care in speech.
The source section's barrier image is a hand interposed against aid; this verse sets a boundary against a hand clenched to the neck or opened without measure.
This verse describes believing men and women as allies who urge good, establish prayer, and give zakah; it is a reciprocal-care counterpart to the section's absent prompting and blocked aid.
This verse defines righteousness to include giving wealth to orphans and the needy, then establishing prayer; it joins the section's bodily aid and prayer in a single standard.
This verse directs spending to parents, kin, orphans, miskin, and travelers, specifying human recipients of the section's withheld care.
The verse commands speaking well to people, then care for orphans, prayer, and charity; it gathers the section's missing encouragement and neglected recipients.
This verse says not to give the orphans' properties for bad in exchange for good or consume them with one's own; it protects what the section's interposing hand could block.
This verse makes unjust consumption of orphan property a fire-bound offense, extending the section's bodily rejection into material exploitation.
The section's lost protective circle is answered by a command not to approach an orphan's property except for its good until maturity.
This ayah similarly protects orphan property until maturity; it makes the section's failed guardianship a concrete boundary.
The section shows the vulnerable pushed aside; this verse asks why oppressed men, women, and children are not defended when they call for rescue.
This verse calls for justice toward orphan women and vulnerable children, extending the section's orphan image to unequal protection in family claims.

The verse says to act for the best concerning orphans and explains that sharing life with them is acceptable because they are kin; it answers the section's image of an adult interposed against a child's need.
This ayah assigns obligatory charity to the poor and needy among its recipients, making aid to them an explicit social duty.
The section depicts aid withheld; this verse forbids withholding promised support from a poor relative and urges pardon instead.
The section's ح ض ض urges others toward good; this verse depicts people who are stingy and command stinginess, a direct inversion of mutual prompting toward food.
The section links prayer with withholding aid; this verse depicts spending to be seen by people, matching the surah's neighboring image of ostentatious prayer.
This verse asks what harm there would be in believing and spending from God's provision; it completes the neighboring contrast between commanded stinginess and showy spending.
This verse warns that ostentatious charity is nullified, directly meeting the whole surah's pairing of displayed worship with withheld aid.
This ayah describes a person who withholds when good reaches him; the next verses exempt the praying and specify a known right for the needy.
This ayah exempts the praying from the withholding just named; 70:24-25 specify the known share due to the asker and deprived.
This ayah says the exempted people maintain their prayers; the following verses add a known right in their wealth for the needy.
The section's refusal of small aid meets the stated right in wealth for the asker and deprived, making provision something owed rather than optional.
This verse names the asker and deprived as recipients of that known right, giving the section's blocked aid its human referent.
This verse describes one who gives and fears God, making upward movement toward good a counter-direction to the section's withholding.
The giver's affirmation of the best is specified here; it deepens the contrast between movement toward good and refusal to encourage it.
The giving path is answered with ease; it frames the section's downward shove as one of two opposed directions.
This verse describes the opposite person as withholding and claiming self-sufficiency, a specific mirror of the section's failure to help the needy.
The withholder's denial of the best is named here, showing that refusal of aid is joined to a false account of what matters.
The withholding path ends in hardship; this is a stated reversal of the ease attached to giving in 92:5-7.
The section turns the shove against its perpetrator at judgment; here wrongdoers are dragged through the Fire on their faces.
The section's dictionary gloss for د ع ع includes driving a flock; here deniers are driven in groups to Hell, a Quranic collective scene of forced arrival.
The section's flock-driving gloss is reversed here: the God-fearing are driven in groups to Paradise, a different destination for gathered people.
The section shows people failing to encourage food for the needy; here feeding the miskin, orphan, and captive is the positive action.
The feeders say they seek God's face and want neither reward nor thanks; this counters both the section's withheld aid and its surah's display before people.
This ayah says the feeders fear a difficult day; it connects their food-sharing to the judgment frame of the section.
The next ayah says these feeders are protected from the day's evil; it adds the consequence of the selfless feeding described in 76:8-10.
The reward passage continues with patience and entry into Paradise; this completes the outcome of feeding the vulnerable in 76:8-11.
This verse says the condemned joined in futile talk after naming prayerlessness and failure to feed; it contrasts wasteful speech with the section's missing word of encouragement.
This verse says the Fire calls the one who turned away; it reverses the section's withholding of aid into a scene of being summoned to punishment.
This verse describes the called person as one who amassed and withheld wealth, turning interposed withholding into judgment.
This verse calls for the steep ascent; the next asks what that ascent is, opening a path whose deeds answer the section's refusal to lift the lowly.
This question names the ascent as the subject; 90:13-17 then defines its liberating, feeding, and mutual acts.
The ascent begins with freeing a person from bondage, a concrete lifting of someone constrained.
The ascent includes feeding on a day of hunger, directly opposing the section's failure to urge food for the miskin.
The ascent reaches an orphan who is near kin, making an actual vulnerable person the object of the path's effort.
The ascent reaches a miskin in the dust, giving the section's lowly image a concrete recipient of care.
The section's root ح ض ض is mutual urging toward good; this ayah describes people urging one another toward mercy alongside the orphan and miskin in the ascent.
This ayah identifies people who take the preceding ascent of freeing, feeding, and mutual mercy as companions of the right.
The passage's alternative is people who reject God's signs; this names the rejected path beside the ascent of care in 90:11-18.
The rejected path ends with Fire shut over its people, the adverse boundary to the ascent's companions of the right.
This ayah says the Lord tested a person by expanding provision, which the next verse answers; it introduces the mistaken equation of wealth and honor.
The person says narrowed provision means humiliation; 89:17-18 answer that the test is instead whether the orphan is honored and the miskin fed.
The next ayah adds that they consume inheritance greedily; this sharpens the preceding refusal to feed the poor into active appropriation.
The next ayah names intense love of wealth, explaining the appetite surrounding the orphan's and poor person's neglect.
The section cites a stillness gloss for root س ه و; this verse uses the Quranic plural sāhūn for people immersed in heedlessness, making the related sense explicit.
This verse establishes the garden owners and their planned early harvest; 68:24 discloses that the plan excludes the miskin.
The owners make no exception to their harvest plan; 68:24 identifies the miskin as those excluded.
A visitation overtakes the garden while its owners sleep, reversing their planned harvest before the poor can share in it.
The garden becomes as if harvested; the planned crop for the owners is lost, reversing their effort to exclude the miskin in 68:24.
The owners call one another in the morning; 68:22 gives their instruction to go to the crop and 68:24 reveals the exclusion.
They tell one another to go to their crop; the following whisper and exclusion in 68:23-24 show the purpose of this journey.
The section quotes their whispered walk; 68:24 supplies the content of that whisper, a plan that no miskin enter.
They go out determined and confident in their plan; 68:24 has named the person they mean to keep from the garden.
When they see the destroyed garden, the owners first think they have lost their way; their planned control of the harvest has failed.
They recognize that they have instead been deprived, reversing their effort to deprive the miskin of the crop.
The most measured among them asks why they did not glorify God; this is the first rebuke after their failed exclusion.
They confess they were wrongdoers, explicitly judging their conduct after the garden's loss.
The owners turn to blame one another; this is the social aftermath of their shared plan to exclude the miskin.
They say they transgressed, naming the wrongdoing behind the garden scene.
They hope their Lord will replace the lost garden with something better; this follows their confession after the failed exclusion.
The passage calls this a punishment and says the punishment of the Hereafter is greater, completing the consequence of the garden owners' scheme.

The section's root م ن ع means standing between someone and what they want; this verse uses that root for preventing people from God's mosques and from remembrance there, a parallel barrier aimed at worship.
This verse joins mutual commands toward wrong with hands held back; it reverses the section's mutual urging toward good and its image of a hand interposed against aid.
The section describes the orphan as lacking a protective ring; here the Prophet is recalled as an orphan who was sheltered.
This neighboring ayah says the Prophet was found in need and enriched; it extends the sheltering counter-scene of 93:6 to material need.
The source section names مسكنة as a form of lowliness and weakness; this verse pairs that same word with a people asking for food, linking deprivation to imposed humiliation.
The section names مسكنة as humiliation; this verse uses that same word for a state imposed on a people, a repeated Quranic use of the secondary sense.
The section derives the miskin image from root س ك ن as motion gone; this verse uses the same root for night made a repose, showing its restorative sense beside need-stilled motion.

The section reads stillness of the heart in prayer as neglect; here the same root س ك ن names tranquility sent into believers' hearts, a positive settled state that distinguishes stillness from heedlessness.
The section describes mutual prompting through root ح ض ض; this verse gives a specific reciprocal form, urging one another to truth and patience, though its object is different from feeding the poor.
The section's dictionary gloss for د ع ع includes driving a flock; here two women hold their flock back at a watering place, and 28:24 shows Moses providing the water they lacked.
This ayah shows Moses watering the two women's flock and then acknowledging his own need; it reverses the section's scene of a strong person withholding help from the vulnerable.

The section's secondary gloss pictures telling a person who has stumbled to rise and recover; this verse describes people who wrong themselves, seek forgiveness, and do not persist, a moral recovery parallel.
The section's dictionary image includes a person who stumbles; this ayah describes Adam and his wife being made to slip and expelled from their prior place, with 2:37 supplying the recovery.
After the fall in 2:36, Adam receives words and God accepts his repentance; this supplies a specific return after stumbling.
This question opens the testimony answered in 74:43-46; its contribution is to frame prayerlessness, failure to feed the miskin, and denial as the reasons for reaching Saqar.
This verse says the condemned remained in that state until certainty came, closing the testimony whose failures mirror the section.
This verse describes the prayer at the Sacred House as whistling and clapping; it gives a concrete empty performance opposite the section's concern with a motionless heart in prayer.
This verse says seeking help through prayer is hard except for the humble; it distinguishes the section's still, inattentive heart from prayer marked by inward humility.
The successful believers are described as humble in prayer, a direct inward counterpoint to the section's stillness gloss for the heedless worshipper.
This verse says people are called to spend, yet some withhold; it directly joins a call toward provision with its refusal, and says withholding ultimately harms the withholder.
This repeats the section's specific inversion: miserliness paired with commanding others to be miserly, rather than mutual encouragement toward good.
This verse introduces two gardens as a parable; 18:34-36 develops the owner's boast that wealth and gardens mean security.
This ayah describes the gardens' fruit and flowing water, establishing the provision whose false security the following speech assumes.
The owner boasts of greater wealth and a stronger following; this echoes the section's correction of the claim that expanded provision means divine honor.
The owner enters his garden wronging himself and assumes it will never perish; this makes the section's warning about treating provision as secure concrete.
The owner doubts the Hour but expects an even better return if brought back to God; this links garden wealth to the section's judgment frame.
His companion answers the boast by recalling his creation from dust and a drop; this rebukes the self-made status implied by wealth.
The companion states belief in God as Lord and rejects association; this is the direct faith contrast inside the garden dialogue.
The companion tells him to acknowledge God's will and that power belongs to God when entering the garden; this counters the owner's assumed control of provision.
The companion names the possibility that God may give him something better than the garden; the supposed secure provision is shown to be contingent.
The companion imagines the garden's water sinking beyond reach, a concrete reversal of accessible provision.
The garden is destroyed and the owner turns his hands over what he spent; this reverses the pride and control attached to the garden.
No group can help the owner after the garden's destruction; this contrasts with the section's idea of a protective circle around a vulnerable person.
The passage says true protection belongs to God; it clarifies the section's contrast between a lost protective ring and people who block aid.
This verse introduces Qarun's immense treasure and says he transgressed; it is a specific parallel to the section's question of how abundant provision is used.
Qarun is told to seek the Hereafter with what God gave him, do good as God did good to him, and not spread corruption; this is a direct counter-duty to withholding care.
Qarun says his wealth came from knowledge he possessed; this parallels the mistaken claim that abundance proves honor or self-sufficiency.
The people who desire Qarun's worldly share watch his display; this connects ostentatious appearance with wealth detached from the section's care for the needy.
The knowledgeable answer that God's reward is better for those who believe and act rightly; this corrects the envy of visible wealth in 28:79.
Qarun and his dwelling are swallowed by the earth; this turns abundant provision into a lowly reversal.
The people recognize that God expands and restricts provision as He wills; this states the correction to Qarun's wealth claim and completes the section's provision theme.
